official_sources.finding: Raster band unit metadata may explicitly identify elevation units such as m or ft.
Raster band scale and offset convert raw values to physical units with units_value = raw*scale+offset.
RasterIO and ReadBlock do not automatically apply raster scale and offset.
GetScale success status must be checked because a default value may otherwise be returned.
GetOffset success status must be checked because a default value may otherwise be returned.
An empty raster unit string means the unit is unknown rather than metres by assumption.
GDAL SetUnitType documents m and ft as standard elevation-unit examples.
gdal raster unscale applies stored scale and offset metadata to convert scaled values to unscaled physical values.
Unscale can change output datatype, so physical-unit decoding and numeric dtype must both be pinned.
Raster scaling can clip values unless no-clip is explicit, so scaling is not a neutral unit-label operation.
gdal raster edit can override scale and offset metadata without resampling, so metadata provenance must be immutable.
gdal raster edit can override CRS without reprojection, so CRS labels alone cannot prove coordinate conversion occurred.
GTI metadata can define per-band scale, offset and unit type, so tile-index metadata participates in physical-value interpretation.
Terrain derivatives depend on the ratio between vertical and horizontal units.
GDAL can infer slope scaling from CRS axis units and raster band unit metadata when recognized.
Metres, international feet and US survey feet are treated as distinct unit cases in terrain-unit handling.
PROJ unitconvert supports explicit vertical z_in and z_out units.
PROJ linear-unit conversion factors are defined relative to metres.
PROJ distinguishes international foot from US survey foot.
Unit conversion may be represented as an explicit pipeline step rather than an implicit numeric assumption.
Vertical CRS operations may require only axis/unit conversion when datums are otherwise compatible.
PROJ distinguishes vertical height from depth through axis direction.
Fallback vertical transformations may be marked ballpark and have unknown accuracy.
Compound CRS operation construction considers horizontal and vertical components separately before chaining.
A VerticalCRS models gravity-related height or depth with a one-dimensional vertical coordinate system.
Ellipsoidal height is not represented as a standalone VerticalCRS but as part of a geographic 3D coordinate tuple.
CompoundCRS is composed from independent component CRSs.
PROJJSON represents vertical axis direction and unit explicitly.
A PROJJSON CompoundCRS can carry a distinct vertical CRS component with its own datum and axis.
Coordinate-system axis direction explicitly distinguishes UP from DOWN.
Coordinate values are to be recorded using the unit defined for their coordinate-system axis.
Changing CRS linear units can either convert existing values or merely override the unit label; these are semantically different.
Promoting a 2D CRS to 3D introduces an ellipsoidal-height axis oriented upward in metres.
PROJ provides an explicit API to construct a CompoundCRS from horizontal and vertical components.
PROJ axis orientation distinguishes easting/northing/up from alternatives including down.
A geodetic transformation pipeline may contain explicit z-unit conversion and vertical-grid-shift steps.
Environment Agency Time Stamped DTM elevations are presented in metres.
Environment Agency Time Stamped DTM elevations are referenced to Ordnance Datum Newlyn/Newlyn.
Environment Agency Time Stamped DTM is aligned to the Ordnance Survey Grid.
Environment Agency reports ±15 cm RMSE vertical accuracy for the LIDAR dataset.
Environment Agency Time Stamped DTM is distributed as GeoTIFF raster data.
The dataset is available at multiple resolutions, so unit identity must not be inferred from resolution.
OSGM15 absolute accuracy is documented at about 8 mm RMS for mainland Britain.
OSGM15 relative error over a 10 km extent is described as only a few millimetres.
Precise GNSS height determination is a distinct accuracy problem from horizontal positioning.
Approximate raster statistics may use overviews or subsets and therefore cannot serve as exact terminal extrema.
PAM raster metadata can carry scale, offset and unit semantics, so sidecar-derived metadata must be provenance-bound.
PROJ supports centimetre, millimetre, decimetre and kilometre as distinct linear units in addition to metre.
PROJ supports international inch, yard, mile and other distance units, so free-text unit aliases should not be guessed.
A vertical operation can differ solely by units or axis direction, meaning equal numeric values do not prove equal heights.
Vertical CRS axis metadata includes an abbreviation, direction and unit that should survive canonical serialization.
Physical-unit extrema must be computed after scale/offset decoding when stored raster values are scaled integers.
Raw-value equality does not imply physical-value equality when scale or offset differs.
Vertical z-unit conversion must be pinned independently from horizontal xy-unit conversion.
